hints: Remember this question asks for two different things at once, a faster rate and a larger equilibrium yield, so test each change against both ideas.
Count the gas moles, 4 moles on the left to 2 moles on the right, and note the forward reaction is exothermic with $\Delta H = -92 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.
Look for the change that both squeezes more particles together for faster collisions and shifts equilibrium toward the side with fewer gas moles.
walkthrough:
**Separate rate from yield**

Think like a teacher with two checklists. Rate is about how fast particles collide successfully. Yield is about where equilibrium lies.

A change can help one but hurt the other, so we need one that helps both.

**Apply Le Chatelier to the equilibrium**

The equation is:
$$\text{N}_2(\text{g}) + 3\text{H}_2(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(\text{g})$$
Left side has 4 gas moles, right side has 2 gas moles. Forward reaction is exothermic.

So high pressure favours the right (fewer moles), and low temperature favours the right (exothermic direction).

**Check rate effects**

Higher temperature, higher pressure (higher concentration), and more catalyst surface all increase rate. Lower temperature decreases rate. A catalyst never changes the position of equilibrium.

Only increased pressure passes both tests: faster collisions and equilibrium shifted to $\text{NH}_3$.

options.A: A decrease in temperature does increase the equilibrium yield because the exothermic forward reaction is favoured at low temperature, but it decreases the rate because particles have less kinetic energy and fewer successful collisions per second.
options.B: An increase in temperature does increase the rate because of more frequent and more energetic collisions, but it decreases the equilibrium yield because equilibrium shifts left toward the endothermic direction, away from $\text{NH}_3$.
options.C: An increase in pressure increases rate because the gases are more concentrated, so collision frequency increases. It also increases equilibrium yield because equilibrium shifts to the side with fewer gas moles, 4 moles to 2 moles, which is the $\text{NH}_3$ side.
options.D: Increasing catalyst surface area increases the rate by providing more active sites and lowering activation energy for both forward and reverse reactions, but it has no effect on the position of equilibrium, so the yield of ammonia is unchanged.
